title: Pelvic floor therapy: what to expect at your first appointment
seoTitle: Pelvic Floor Therapy: What to Expect at Your First Visit
description: Prepare for pelvic floor therapy with a clear guide to the first visit, examination choices, questions to bring and what a useful home plan looks like.
excerpt: Know what the conversation, examination and treatment plan can involve—and the choices you have throughout.
quickAnswer: A first pelvic floor therapy appointment usually begins with your symptoms, health history and goals. An examination may be offered, including an internal assessment when relevant, but it requires your consent. Treatment can include education and individualized exercises. You can ask for explanations, discuss alternatives and request a chaperone.
takeaways: Bring examples of the activities your symptoms affect.
An internal examination is a choice to discuss, not a test you must pass.
Leave knowing what to practice, what to stop and how follow-up works.

sections.title: Before you book or attend
sections.html:
Pelvic health physiotherapists work with bladder, bowel, sexual and pregnancy-related problems. You do not need to know which muscle is responsible before seeking help. University Hospitals Sussex explains the scope of pelvic health care.

When booking, check whether the appointment is by phone, video or in person, how long to allow, and whether you should complete any forms. A remote first appointment can gather your history and explain possible examinations; an in-person visit may follow if needed, as described by DynamicHealth's NHS service. Policies vary, so use your own clinic's instructions.

If you need an interpreter, accessible room, support person or particular communication approach, ask in advance. You do not need to wait until an uncomfortable moment to explain what would help.

If the clinic sends a questionnaire that feels difficult to complete, note the questions you would rather discuss in person. Bringing an incomplete form is preferable to inventing an answer.

sections.title: The first conversation: what matters to you?
sections.html:
Expect questions about symptoms, previous treatment and relevant medical history. Rather than searching for the correct medical term, bring examples: “I leak when I lift my toddler,” “I feel pressure after standing,” or “penetration hurts at the entrance.” These tell a clearer story than “my pelvic floor is bad.”

Prepare a short page with:

  • When the concern began and whether it has changed.
  • Activities that bring it on or ease it.
  • Relevant surgery, pregnancies, births and medications.
  • Exercises or products you have already tried.
  • The activity you most want to make easier.

Birmingham Women's and Children's NHS recommends bringing relevant letters, medication details and any requested diary or questionnaire. If you have been asked to complete a bladder diary, bring the actual record; you do not need to summarize it perfectly.

sections.title: What if symptoms flare after a session or home exercise?
sections.html:
Tell your therapist about a new or stronger symptom before repeating the activity that provokes it. Do not assume that soreness proves a treatment worked, or that a flare automatically proves damage. The response needs context. East Lancashire Hospitals advises specialist review for pain during or after pelvic floor exercise.

Use a short message that makes the change easy to assess: “After the session on [day], I noticed [symptom] at [time]. It affects [activity]. It is now improving, unchanged or worsening. Should I pause this part of the plan until we speak?” Include which home exercises you actually did, without repeating a painful exercise to test it.

Ask whether the next session should change the dose, the movement, manual treatment or the order of activities. Agree on the expected response and a contact route if symptoms exceed it. You can ask to stop a technique during an appointment and discuss another approach.

Do not wait for the clinic to reply if symptoms need urgent care. NHS guidance advises emergency care for severe or worsening pelvic pain or pain with faintness, and urgent medical advice for pelvic pain with fever or difficulty passing urine. These symptoms should not be dismissed as routine post-treatment soreness.

sections.title: What if you are told stress is preventing progress?
sections.html:
Stress deserves a place in the care discussion without making your pain less real. RCOG describes long-term pelvic pain as potentially involving physical, psychological and social factors, and emphasizes an agreed management plan. ACOG describes care that may involve several specialties, including physical therapy and mental health support.

If a clinician recommends pausing physiotherapy, ask for the clinical reason and the next step in writing. A useful question is: “Which part of treatment are we pausing, what needs to change before we review it, and who will help me in the meantime?” Distinguish a pause in one technique from losing all support.

Bring the practical barriers into the conversation: appointment cost, sleep, work, transport or difficulty following a complex home plan. Ask whether the plan can be simplified or coordinated with your existing clinician. You do not need a perfectly calm life before describing pain and requesting an explanation.

If the explanation is unclear or the plan leaves you without follow-up, ask your primary-care clinician about review or another appropriately qualified service. Our care-access guide includes questions about referrals, costs and appointment formats. This is a way to clarify care; it cannot determine why an individual clinician recommended stopping a treatment.

sections.title: What might an examination involve?
sections.html:
The assessment depends on your concern. It may look at movement and the painful area; a vaginal or rectal examination may be proposed to assess pelvic floor function. Imperial College Healthcare describes this individualized process.

Before agreeing, ask what the examination will assess and how the result would change treatment. You can say, “Please explain each step before you do it,” or “I would like to discuss the examination today and decide later.” Tell the clinician if a particular position, touch or past experience makes you apprehensive; you can choose how much detail to share.

Sussex's appointment information states that an internal examination is optional and that a chaperone can be provided. Ask your clinic about these arrangements. You can withdraw consent and ask to stop.

sections.title: A decision sheet to take to your therapist
sections.html:
Use this short sheet to turn the conversation into decisions you understand. Write the answers in your own words; it is a preparation tool, not a medical questionnaire.

AskLeave knowing
What will this examination help you assess?What information it adds and how it could affect my plan.
What can we do if I prefer to defer an internal examination?Which parts of assessment or treatment can proceed and what remains uncertain.
What is my home practice meant to change?A practical goal, the movement and the dose.
What should I do if symptoms increase?My stopping rule and contact route.
How will we review progress?What to record and when to arrange follow-up.

University Hospitals Sussex’s appointment information states that patients can still receive treatment if they decline an internal examination, and that consent is also sought before students observe or participate. Ask your own service about its arrangements. Agreeing to attend an appointment does not require you to agree to every proposed step.

This section was added after checking the Sussex information on October 26, 2026.

sections.title: Therapy is more than a list of Kegels
sections.html:
Your plan might include movement practice, education, lifestyle advice or other techniques selected for your findings. Imperial's patient guide describes several treatment approaches rather than one standard routine. Read why tightness and weakness are different questions if you are expecting strengthening automatically.

Ask your therapist to connect each instruction to your goal. “This is intended to help with the leak during lifting” is easier to use than collecting exercises without knowing their purpose. If the plan is too complicated to fit around work or caring responsibilities, say so before leaving.

sections.title: Can the first plan start without internal work?
sections.html:
Tell the service before the visit if you want to start with conversation and activities that keep you clothed. You can ask what information they can gather from your history, symptom diary, breathing and relevant movement, and which proposed steps would need separate consent. DynamicHealth’s NHS service describes remote first appointments and individually tailored management; your own clinic can explain its options.

External treatment is not one standardized package, and no appointment guide can promise the same relief as every other approach. Ask the therapist to explain what they can assess now, what remains uncertain, and what would make them recommend further assessment. Declining an examination does not require replacing it with unsupervised internal work at home.

A useful opening sentence is: “I want help with these symptoms, and I am not consenting to an internal examination today. What can we begin with?” You can also request a chaperone or ask how a support person could attend.

The Chartered Society of Physiotherapy describes informed consent as an ongoing process. Agree on a review point for the plan you choose; improvement is assessed against your goals, not your willingness to accept a particular examination.

sections.title: Leave with a plan you can repeat accurately
sections.html:
For each exercise, record the position, movement, repetitions, rest and frequency. Ask what discomfort should make you stop and who to contact with questions. Demonstrate or explain the instructions back in your own words so that any misunderstanding can be corrected while you are together.

Finally, confirm the follow-up arrangement: whether you must book it, what to track and when the approach will be reviewed. Keep a note of one useful change in daily life as well as what you practiced. If nothing changes, that information belongs at the review too. Therapy is a process of assessment and adjustment; your job is to give an honest account, not to produce a perfect progress report.

faqs.question: Do I have to have an internal examination?
faqs.answer: No. Ask why it is being offered, discuss alternatives and decide whether to consent. Declining may limit what can be assessed, but you can still discuss symptoms and appropriate care.

faqs.question: Should I cancel if I am on my period?
faqs.answer: Some pelvic health services can still see you during your period. Check your clinic’s policy and your own comfort rather than assuming cancellation is necessary.

faqs.question: What if I agree to talk but am not ready for an internal examination?
faqs.answer: Say that at the start. Ask what can be assessed now, what would remain uncertain and whether you can revisit the decision later. Discuss your own service’s options without feeling you must decide before receiving an explanation.

faqs.question: Can I ask to begin therapy while staying clothed?
faqs.answer: Yes. Tell the clinic your preference and ask what assessment and treatment are possible, what remains uncertain, and how the plan will be reviewed. Options depend on your symptoms and the service.

title: Pelvic floor exercises after a C-section: when and how to restart
seoTitle: Pelvic Floor Exercises After a C-Section: Getting Started
description: Learn how pelvic floor care fits after a C-section, when to ask about restarting exercises, what changes the plan and which symptoms need attention.
excerpt: Caesarean recovery includes the pelvic floor as well as the abdominal incision. Start with the guidance for your own birth.
quickAnswer: Pelvic floor care can still matter after a C-section because pregnancy also affects the pelvic floor. Gentle exercises may begin when comfortable and advised by your maternity team, after any urinary catheter is removed. Difficulty passing urine, pain or complications change the plan; a generic workout should not override your discharge instructions.
takeaways: A C-section does not make pelvic floor symptoms irrelevant.
Wait until a urinary catheter is removed and report emptying problems.
Restarting gentle practice is different from returning to strenuous exercise.

sections.title: Why the pelvic floor still matters
sections.html:
A caesarean avoids a vaginal birth, but the pelvic floor has still supported a pregnancy. You may have questions about leaks, pressure or muscle control even if the abdominal incision is the most obvious part of recovery. Lancashire Teaching Hospitals' caesarean information includes pelvic floor rehabilitation for this reason.

There is no need to compare yourself with someone who had a different delivery, or to interpret symptoms as evidence that your birth “should have prevented” them. Start with what you notice and what your team has advised. Write down whether the issue is leaking, discomfort, uncertainty about movement or difficulty emptying, because each deserves a clear description.

sections.title: When can I restart gentle exercises?
sections.html:
University College London Hospitals includes gentle pelvic floor exercise after caesarean birth and says to wait until a urinary catheter has been removed. Your own maternity team's instructions take priority, particularly if the birth or recovery was complicated.

Before you begin, check three practical points: whether your catheter is out, whether you are passing urine normally, and whether you have been given any individual restrictions. If emptying is difficult, tell the team rather than trying extra squeezes. Ask for help if you are unsure what they mean by “gentle.”

Getting permission for pelvic floor practice is not the same as being ready for a strenuous workout. Keep those decisions separate when asking about recovery.

sections.title: Make the first practice about clear movement
sections.html:
In a comfortable supported position, the movement is a small internal lift followed by a complete letting-go. Keep breathing. Use the amount of practice your clinician recommends and stop if it hurts. UCLH's post-birth exercise advice also warns against exercising by stopping and starting urine flow.

You may find it useful to separate learning from counting. First understand what the intended movement feels like; then write down the routine you have been given. Do not try to demonstrate progress by making a forceful abdominal brace or finishing a timer despite discomfort.

If sensation is unclear, describe that at your next contact. “I cannot tell when the lift ends” is a useful question. Our Kegel technique guide explains the language, while an assessment checks what your body is doing.

sections.title: Fit pelvic floor care into the whole recovery plan
sections.html:
The NHS caesarean recovery guide encourages gentle movement while cautioning against overexertion. Activities such as lifting more than your baby or returning to exercise may need to wait until you feel able and they are comfortable; your midwife can advise.

For planning, divide your day into essential care, optional activity and tasks someone else can do. Feeding your baby, getting to the toilet and resting may already require substantial organization. Put a brief prescribed practice into a manageable gap rather than making it compete with an ambitious fitness schedule.

  • Keep discharge instructions and contact details together.
  • Ask for help with shopping, laundry and older children's needs.
  • Record the activity connected to a symptom, not only its intensity.
  • Discuss changes before adding weights, internal devices or demanding exercise.

Choose one person who can help keep track of appointments or instructions if you are tired. They can write down questions while you focus on your recovery and your baby.

sections.title: Which symptoms should I report?
sections.html:
Contact your maternity team urgently about painful urination, worsening wound redness, pus, severe pain, heavy bleeding, or new calf pain or swelling. Report urine leakage too. These are among the symptoms the NHS says need medical advice after caesarean birth. They should not be treated as a normal response to pelvic floor practice.

New chest pain or sudden breathlessness after surgery needs immediate medical help; call your local emergency service. NHS guidance on pulmonary embolism flags these symptoms as possible signs of a clot in the lungs.

For ongoing non-urgent concerns, use a review to agree the next step: technique support, pelvic health physiotherapy, or a change in the recovery plan. Read our wider postpartum recovery guide for questions to take with you.

faqs.question: Do I need to wait six weeks for every pelvic floor exercise?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Gentle pelvic floor practice and strenuous activity have different considerations. Follow your maternity team’s advice, wait for catheter removal, and raise pain or emptying problems before starting.

faqs.question: Will Kegels help my C-section scar heal?
faqs.answer: Pelvic floor practice is not a substitute for incision care or a full postoperative plan. Follow the wound-care instructions and report changes that concern you.

title: Pelvic floor exercises during pregnancy: a thoughtful starting plan
seoTitle: Pelvic Floor Exercises During Pregnancy: A Practical Guide
description: Explore pelvic floor exercises in pregnancy, what the evidence says about leaks, comfortable positions, full relaxation and questions for your midwife.
excerpt: Understand what pregnancy practice can help with, then adapt it to your comfort, symptoms and maternity advice.
quickAnswer: Pelvic floor training during pregnancy can help prevent urinary leakage in some women, but it is not a guarantee and does not replace assessment of symptoms. Learn a gentle lift and full release, keep breathing and choose a comfortable position. Ask your maternity team to adapt practice if you have pain or exercise restrictions.
takeaways: Prevention evidence is stronger than promises of a guaranteed birth outcome.
Position, comfort and relaxation matter as pregnancy progresses.
New symptoms belong in the maternity conversation, not just a workout log.

sections.title: What can exercises help with?
sections.html:
Pelvic floor training is often included in pregnancy care to support bladder control. A Cochrane review published in 2020 found that pregnant women who were not leaking and undertook preventive training probably had fewer leaks later in pregnancy. Evidence for treating existing pregnancy-related leakage was less certain, and longer-term findings were limited.

That distinction matters. Preventing a problem and treating an established symptom are different questions. If you already leak, tell your midwife so you can discuss appropriate assessment and support rather than assuming the preventive routine is all you need.

Keep your expectations practical: learning the movement, following a suitable plan and asking about symptoms. This article does not promise an easier delivery, no tearing or a particular recovery speed.

sections.title: Learn the lift and the release
sections.html:
Health New Zealand's pregnancy exercise guidance describes closing around the back passage and vagina, lifting inward, then relaxing. Keep breathing and avoid turning the attempt into a buttock squeeze. Do the exercise away from urination; stopping urine flow is not a practice routine.

Ask your midwife or pelvic health physiotherapist to help if the sensation is unclear. Your first useful question may be “How do I know I have let go?” rather than “How many can I do?” Write down the starting amount, rest periods and how to progress, especially if a previous pregnancy or pelvic condition has left you with different advice.

Our technique guide can help you understand the instructions you receive. It cannot check the movement for you.

sections.title: Choose a position that stays comfortable
sections.html:
Supported sitting or side-lying can avoid the need to spend a long time flat on your back. The NHS advises avoiding prolonged flat-back exercise in later pregnancy and stopping activity if you feel uncomfortable or unwell. A growing bump may change which positions work for you.

Do not treat a position change as losing progress. You are trying to practice a specific movement comfortably, not earn a harder version. If you have pelvic girdle pain or another restriction, ask which position your team recommends. The guide to exercise positions explains general differences, but pregnancy advice takes priority.

sections.title: Make a small plan you can revisit
sections.html:
Choose a reminder that survives changes in your day. If morning nausea makes an early session impractical, discuss a more workable schedule. If you have been given a programme, keep that one set of instructions rather than combining several online routines.

A simple weekly note can contain four entries:

  • Practice: the routine you were actually able to follow.
  • Comfort: whether the position and movement remained comfortable.
  • Symptoms: any leakage, pressure, pain or emptying difficulty.
  • Question: one thing to clarify at the next maternity contact.

This is a communication tool, not a scorecard. A new symptom is useful information even when you have followed the plan exactly. Avoid making your routine harder just because the pregnancy is further along.

At your next visit, mention any instruction you have found difficult to follow. A plan that works on paper may need adjustment around nausea, sleep, work or caring responsibilities.

sections.title: When should I speak to my maternity team?
sections.html:
Leeds' perinatal physiotherapy service describes help for bladder and bowel leakage, prolapse symptoms and pregnancy-related pain. Ask about local support if these concerns affect daily life. Pain during pelvic floor practice is a reason to pause and ask for individual advice.

Bleeding, suspected amniotic-fluid leakage or regular painful contractions are reasons to stop exercise and contact your maternity service promptly. ACOG includes these in its pregnancy exercise warning signs. Do not assume a new watery leak is urine if you are unsure. Severe symptoms such as chest pain or marked breathlessness need emergency care.

Keep your maternity contact details easy to find. Knowing where to get advice is part of a useful pregnancy exercise plan, alongside any daily practice.

faqs.question: Can I start if I have never done Kegels before?
faqs.answer: Ask your maternity team how to begin and whether you need technique support or modifications. Start with understanding the movement rather than copying the maximum count in a general guide.

faqs.question: Do I need to keep my pelvic floor clenched to support the baby?
faqs.answer: No. A practice routine includes releasing the muscles between contractions. Do not deliberately hold a constant squeeze throughout the day.

title: Pelvic floor exercises after hysterectomy: restarting with your care plan
seoTitle: Pelvic Floor Exercises After Hysterectomy: Restarting Safely
description: Understand when pelvic floor exercises may restart after hysterectomy, why catheter and bladder recovery matter, and what to clarify before going home.
excerpt: Use your operation details and discharge advice to restart gentle practice and plan a gradual return to daily life.
quickAnswer: After hysterectomy, gentle pelvic floor exercises may be introduced once a urinary catheter is removed and you can pass urine normally, following your surgical team’s advice. The operation type, additional repairs and complications matter. Early muscle practice does not mean internal devices, heavy lifting or strenuous exercise are appropriate.
takeaways: Your exact operation and discharge instructions determine the next step.
Do not practice with a urinary catheter in place or ignore emptying problems.
Gentle muscle practice and the return to heavy activity are separate decisions.

sections.title: Start with the operation you actually had
sections.html:
A hysterectomy can be performed through an abdominal incision, vaginally or using laparoscopy. Recovery varies, and additional procedures can change your restrictions. The NHS recovery guide describes different hospital stays and recovery expectations by approach. A date from someone else's experience is not a reliable clearance for you.

Before leaving hospital, keep a copy of the operation and discharge information. Check whether you had a prolapse repair or another procedure alongside the hysterectomy. These details help anyone advising you later understand which tissues are healing and which instructions apply.

If a leaflet and a verbal instruction appear to conflict, ask the surgical team to resolve it. Do not choose the more demanding option simply because you feel keen to get moving.

sections.title: When might gentle practice restart?
sections.html:
Leeds Teaching Hospitals advises starting pelvic floor exercises gently after the catheter is removed and you can pass urine independently. If you still have a vaginal pack, follow the team's instructions about its removal before practice. Doncaster and Bassetlaw's postoperative guidance specifically says not to start while a catheter or pack remains in place.

Ask the ward team to confirm your starting point rather than trying to remove or work around any device yourself. If urination is difficult after catheter removal, report it. Pelvic floor contractions are not a way to force the bladder to empty.

Your first programme may be modest. The purpose is to regain an appropriate movement, not to prove how much effort you can tolerate immediately after surgery.

sections.title: What should the movement involve?
sections.html:
North Bristol NHS Trust describes an inward and upward contraction around the back passage and vagina, followed by a release to the starting position. It also advises against training by interrupting the urine stream.

Use the hold, rest and repetition count your clinician gives you. Ask for a demonstration or technique check if the words are unclear, and pause if an exercise causes pain. Keep the rest interval in your written instructions: it is easy to remember the number of squeezes and forget what happens between them.

Do not add vaginal weights, a probe or an internal stretching routine because it appears in a general recovery video. Obtain specific advice about when vaginal insertion is appropriate after your operation. External muscle practice and inserting a device are different activities.

sections.title: Plan daily activity separately from exercise repetitions
sections.html:
The NHS encourages early short walks as part of postoperative care while emphasizing the time needed for tissue healing. “I can do my pelvic floor practice” does not answer whether you can lift a full laundry basket, resume your gym class or return to a physical job.

Make a practical list of the jobs waiting at home. Include pet care, shopping, changing bedding and anything involving children. Ask which tasks need help and for how long. Agree a way to increase activity and a review point, rather than treating one good morning as clearance for everything.

Ask about constipation management as well. RCOG's abdominal hysterectomy guide discusses keeping stools easy to pass and the possible need for laxatives. Follow the medication advice you were given; do not strain to finish a bowel movement.

sections.title: What needs a call rather than another workout?
sections.html:
Contact your surgical service promptly for increasing abdominal pain, heavy or unpleasant-smelling bleeding, wound redness or painful urination. Fever or vomiting alongside worsening pain also needs assessment. RCOG lists these in its postoperative warning signs. New chest pain, breathlessness or coughing blood requires immediate medical help.

At a routine review, discuss function as well as healing: walking comfort, bladder and bowel control, pressure symptoms and the activities you want to resume. If exercises remain confusing or symptoms persist, ask whether pelvic health physiotherapy would help. A clear plan should tell you both what to do next and what information would make the team reconsider it.

faqs.question: Does removing the uterus remove the need for pelvic floor care?
faqs.answer: No. The pelvic floor still has roles in bladder and bowel control and support. Discuss symptoms and an appropriate rehabilitation plan with your team.

faqs.question: Can I use my usual vaginal trainer straight after surgery?
faqs.answer: Do not resume an internal device without specific postoperative advice. The timing depends on healing and the procedures you had; gentle external contractions do not establish that insertion is safe.

title: Exercise with pelvic organ prolapse: a practical guide to staying active
seoTitle: Exercise With Pelvic Organ Prolapse: Practical Next Steps
description: Learn where pelvic floor exercise fits in prolapse care, how to discuss activity modifications, what a pessary does and which symptoms need review.
excerpt: Discuss movement, muscle training and other support options without relying on a universal list of safe exercises.
quickAnswer: Pelvic floor training may improve prolapse symptoms, but exercise does not guarantee that a prolapse will disappear. A clinician can assess the type of prolapse and help adapt activity. Comfortable lower-impact options, symptom tracking and discussion of a support pessary may be useful parts of an individualized plan.
takeaways: A prolapse diagnosis does not tell you everything about your activity needs.
Symptom improvement and a guaranteed anatomical cure are different outcomes.
Training, activity adjustments and pessaries can be discussed together.

sections.title: Understand what your diagnosis means
sections.html:
Pelvic organ prolapse occurs when pelvic organs bulge toward or into the vagina as their support changes. Symptoms can include a bulge, heaviness, bladder or bowel difficulties, although some prolapses cause few symptoms. The NHS prolapse guide recommends assessment for a vaginal lump or other prolapse symptoms.

Ask which structures are involved and what the findings mean for your daily life. A name or stage is useful medical information, but it does not explain how a long shift, lifting a child or a favorite class feels to you. Bring those examples into the discussion.

If you discovered a bulge yourself, do not begin repeated internal checks to decide whether exercise is “fixing” it. Arrange assessment and agree how progress will be evaluated.

sections.title: What can pelvic floor training realistically do?
sections.html:
Gloucestershire Hospitals describes pelvic floor exercise as a way to improve symptoms in mild to moderate prolapse, while cautioning that exercises are unlikely to cure a large prolapse. The aim should be a useful improvement in function and comfort, not a promised reversal from a video or product.

A pelvic health physiotherapist can help choose a programme and assess technique. Ask how to coordinate the lift and full release, what dose to use and what to do if practice brings on pain or pressure. If you already have a plan, do not add a second routine because its title mentions prolapse.

Track the activity you care about: perhaps standing to cook or walking to the shops. That gives the review a practical focus beyond the number of repetitions completed.

sections.title: Choose activities you can discuss and adjust
sections.html:
The NHS advises avoiding activities that put substantial strain on the pelvic floor, including heavy lifting and high-impact exercise. Royal Berkshire's exercise leaflet lists options such as swimming, walking, water-based classes and seated cycling. These are starting points for discussion, not a guarantee that every version suits every person.

Instead of asking only “Is this exercise safe?”, give your clinician the details: the class length, whether it includes jumping, the load you lift and what you feel during and afterward. A short gentle session and a demanding class can share the same activity name.

Agree which variable to adjust first. You might discuss duration, impact or load rather than changing everything simultaneously. If symptoms are noticeably worse, reduce the provoking activity and arrange advice rather than pushing through to test your limits.

sections.title: Use a simple activity record
sections.html:
A short record can make an exercise discussion more specific. For a few typical activities, note:

What you didWhat to record
Walk or classDuration, impact and how symptoms behaved.
Home or work taskThe object, repeated lifts or time spent standing.
AfterwardWhether discomfort settled or affected the rest of the day.

This is not a way to assign yourself a stage or declare an activity harmless. It gives your clinician something concrete to work with. Include activities you enjoy and need to keep doing, so the plan can address real priorities rather than simply shrinking your life.

sections.title: Where do pessaries and other care fit?
sections.html:
A vaginal pessary is a fitted support device, not a training weight. RCOG describes physiotherapy, pessaries and surgery as options chosen according to symptoms and preferences. Not everyone with prolapse needs an operation.

If symptoms limit activity, ask whether a pessary might be appropriate and what fitting, removal and follow-up would involve. Also discuss constipation and a persistent cough; Gloucestershire's guidance includes addressing these repeated sources of strain.

Report changing bladder emptying, new pain or unexpected bleeding rather than attributing everything to an established diagnosis. Sudden inability to pass urine needs immediate medical care; see NIDDK’s urinary retention guidance. For ongoing questions, our physiotherapy appointment guide can help you prepare. A useful plan makes room for review and more than one treatment option.

faqs.question: Will Kegels push a prolapse back into place permanently?
faqs.answer: That is not a reliable promise. Training may help symptoms and support function, but the response depends on the prolapse and individual circumstances. Discuss realistic goals with your clinician.

faqs.question: Is a pessary the same as a vaginal weight?
faqs.answer: No. A pessary supports a prolapse and is fitted for that purpose. A vaginal weight is used in some exercise programmes. Do not substitute one for the other.

title: Painful sex and the pelvic floor: what to discuss and what may help
seoTitle: Painful Sex and the Pelvic Floor: Causes and Support
description: Understand how pelvic floor muscles can contribute to painful sex, why other causes need checking, and how to seek care without pushing through pain.
excerpt: Pain during sex deserves an explanation and a care plan. Stronger contractions are not automatically the answer.
quickAnswer: Pelvic floor muscles can contribute to painful sex, particularly when they tighten involuntarily or have difficulty relaxing. Pain can also come from tissue changes, infection, skin conditions or other pelvic problems. Frequent or severe pain deserves assessment. Avoid forcing painful penetration or starting a strengthening routine to solve an unknown cause.
takeaways: Pain is a reason to change the approach, not a requirement for progress.
Muscles may be involved, but a matching symptom does not establish the cause.
Your examination and treatment should respect your choices and comfort.

sections.title: The pelvic floor is one possible part of the explanation
sections.html:
Pain with sex may be felt at the entrance, deeper inside the pelvis, or afterward. ACOG describes several possible causes, including hormonal tissue changes, skin conditions, infection, childbirth-related problems and conditions such as endometriosis. More than one factor can matter.

Before choosing an exercise, describe the pattern. Is the discomfort associated with touch at the entrance, deeper penetration, a particular position or the time afterward? Does dryness seem relevant? Do tampons or examinations also hurt? These observations can help a clinician decide what to assess; they cannot identify the cause by themselves.

You do not have to prove that the pain is severe enough to deserve help. If it changes what you are comfortable doing, it belongs in the conversation.

sections.title: When muscle tightening is involved
sections.html:
With vaginismus, muscles tighten involuntarily around attempted vaginal insertion. It can happen with penetration, a tampon or an examination, and it is not something a person chooses. The NHS explains this automatic response and describes specialist treatment that may combine education, relaxation and other approaches.

A description that sounds familiar is not a diagnosis. Pain at the vulva can also occur without an obvious visible change; the NHS vulvodynia guide explains why persistent or recurring vulval pain needs assessment. You should not have to see a lesion or swelling before asking for care.

Our tight-versus-weak guide explains why squeezing harder is not an appropriate default response to pain. The useful question is what treatment fits the findings.

sections.title: Burning at the vaginal entrance: what to explain
sections.html:
Tell the clinician whether pain starts with light touch at the entrance, attempted insertion, deeper penetration or afterward. These are useful distinctions for assessment, not a way to diagnose yourself. You do not need to repeat a painful attempt to demonstrate the symptom.

NHS guidance on vulvodynia explains that vulval pain can feel burning or sore even when the skin looks normal. Infection and other conditions may also cause pain there, so a normal-looking area does not establish that it is only a muscle problem.

Bring a brief description of the first point at which pain begins and any associated dryness, discharge, skin changes or urinary symptoms. Ask what an examination would involve, how to pause it and whether tests are needed to exclude another cause. You can discuss an examination before consenting to it.

Persistent or recurring pain, painful sex or difficulty with tampon insertion is a reason to seek care. Although a chronic pain diagnosis may use a duration threshold, you do not need to wait months before asking for help. Pause activities that hurt while you arrange assessment; a strengthening app is not a treatment for unexplained entrance burning.

sections.title: Protect comfort while arranging care
sections.html:
You can pause penetration or choose activities that do not hurt. ACOG's sexual health guidance discusses allowing time for arousal, using appropriate lubricant and considering activities without penetration. If using condoms, check lubricant compatibility; water-based or silicone options are generally appropriate, while oils can damage latex.

Agree on an easy way to stop or change activity before it starts. For example: “If I say pause, I need us to stop and check in.” You do not owe anyone a further attempt to see whether the pain will disappear. A supportive conversation can focus on what feels comfortable now, without making penetration the measure of success.

Lubricant may reduce friction, but persistent pain still needs investigation. Do not repeatedly treat presumed thrush, insert weights or force a stretch without understanding the problem. Bring the names of any products you have tried to the appointment.

sections.title: Make the assessment easier to use
sections.html:
ACOG advises seeing a clinician for frequent or severe pain during sex. Assessment may include your medical and sexual history, an examination and tests when appropriate. See its guide to painful sex.

You can prepare a brief note rather than explaining everything from memory:

  • Where the pain is and what it feels like.
  • When it began and whether it is changing.
  • Any bleeding, discharge, urinary symptoms or skin changes.
  • Relevant childbirth, surgery, medications or menopause symptoms.
  • What you want to be able to do comfortably.

Before an examination, discuss what is proposed and what would help you feel in control. Ask about a chaperone or support person and explain that you want each step described. Our pelvic health appointment guide outlines the choices involved.

sections.title: What might treatment involve?
sections.html:
Treatment depends on the cause. The NHS describes care involving different specialists for vulval pain, with options that may include medication, physiotherapy and psychological or psychosexual therapies. This does not mean the pain is imaginary; it means care may need to address several aspects of the experience.

Vaginal trainers or dilators may be used in some specialist plans, but they are not the same as strengthening weights. The NHS vaginismus guidance places their initial use under trained supervision. Ask what the tool is for, how to use it comfortably and when to stop.

Review progress using your own priorities, such as less discomfort with daily touch or greater comfort during an examination. There is no requirement to achieve a particular sexual activity by a deadline. If the plan increases pain or feels unmanageable, return for an adjustment.

faqs.question: Should I do more Kegels if sex hurts?
faqs.answer: Not without understanding the cause. Stronger contractions are not a general treatment for painful sex. Seek assessment and ask whether your muscles need help with relaxation, coordination or another issue.

faqs.question: Do vaginal trainers mean I have to push through discomfort?
faqs.answer: No. Ask a qualified clinician for an individualized plan and clear stopping rules. A trainer is not a test of how much pain you can tolerate.

faqs.question: Can burning at the entrance need assessment when the skin looks normal?
faqs.answer: Yes. Persistent or recurring vulval pain or pain with penetration deserves care even without an obvious visible change. You do not need to wait months before asking for help.

title: Kegel weights and pelvic floor trainers: what to know before buying
seoTitle: Kegel Weights and Trainers: Evidence and Buying Questions
description: Compare pelvic floor weights, biofeedback and stimulation devices, understand the evidence, and use a practical checklist before buying a trainer.
excerpt: Different devices solve different problems. Start with the purpose, evidence and suitability before comparing features.
quickAnswer: Kegel weights, biofeedback trainers and electrical stimulators are different tools. None is automatically necessary or better than a well-taught exercise programme. A clinician can help identify whether a device suits your symptoms and technique. Pregnancy, recent surgery, pain or difficulty with insertion are reasons to get specific advice before use.
takeaways: A weight, sensor and electrical stimulator do different jobs.
A higher device score is not the same as fewer symptoms.
Check suitability, instructions and evidence before choosing a product.

sections.title: First, identify what the device actually does
sections.html:
“Pelvic floor trainer” is a broad marketing label. A product might provide resistance, display a measurement, deliver stimulation or simply guide timing. Before comparing prices, find out which function you are buying.

ToolBasic purpose
Vaginal weight or coneProvides a load to retain during an exercise programme.
Biofeedback deviceShows information about a measured muscle-related signal.
Electrical stimulatorUses electrical stimulation to help produce a contraction.
Timer or reminderOrganizes practice without measuring the muscles.

Northampton General Hospital describes weights, feedback and stimulation as distinct treatment tools. A feature list should make these differences clear. If it does not, ask the manufacturer for the instructions before purchasing.

sections.title: What does research say about weights?
sections.html:
A Cochrane review published in 2013 found some evidence that vaginal cones helped stress incontinence compared with no active treatment. It did not establish a clear advantage over pelvic floor exercise without cones. The trials were small and had limitations, and some women found cones difficult or unpleasant to use.

This is older evidence about a treatment approach, not proof that any current retail product will work for you. Ask whether a claim is based on the exact device, a similar device or pelvic floor training in general. Those are not interchangeable pieces of evidence.

Price, the number of weights and an attractive app do not answer the clinical question. Start with the problem you want to improve and the reason a weight might add value to your existing care.

sections.title: More measurement does not guarantee better results
sections.html:
A 2025 Cochrane review found little or no difference in incontinence-related quality of life when biofeedback was added to pelvic floor training, and probably little or no difference in reported cure or improvement. That does not rule out an individual teaching role, but it does not support a universal promise of superior results.

Ask what a displayed score represents, whether it helps identify relaxation as well as contraction, and how a clinician would interpret it. Track the symptom or activity you care about alongside any device number. A rising graph is not a complete account of bladder control or comfort.

For a closer comparison of reminders and sensors, read Kegel apps versus biofeedback trainers.

sections.title: Check suitability before inserting or switching on
sections.html:
Electrical stimulation has specific precautions. Leeds Teaching Hospitals' NMES guidance requires a physiotherapist to assess suitability and lists situations where its stimulator should not be used, including pregnancy, certain implanted devices and early recovery after birth or surgery. Do not apply a general shopping guide in place of those checks.

For any internal product, ask for advice first if you have pain, unexplained bleeding, infection symptoms, prolapse concerns or recent surgery. A device that is painful to insert is not something to “grow into” by forcing it. Check the exact product's restrictions and your clinician's instructions; one model's schedule should not be copied onto another.

Also distinguish a vaginal weight from a dilator used in some pain-treatment plans and a pessary fitted for prolapse support. Similar placement does not mean the same purpose.

sections.title: A practical checklist before spending money
sections.html:
Make sure you can answer these questions in plain language:

  • What specific problem is this intended to help me address?
  • Who has checked that I can use it appropriately?
  • What does it measure or do, and what can it not tell me?
  • What are the instructions for cleaning, storage, use and stopping?
  • Can I review the instructions and return policy before purchase?
  • Does the connected app collect intimate health information, and can I control or delete it?

If a device is recommended, keep one agreed programme and confirm when it will be reviewed. Do not combine its routine with extra sets from other sources simply to accelerate progress. If the purpose remains unclear, a technique assessment is a more useful next step than choosing the most elaborate model.

faqs.question: Do I need vaginal weights to strengthen my pelvic floor?
faqs.answer: No. They are one possible training tool, not a requirement. Ask whether they add anything useful to your individual plan before buying.

faqs.question: Can I wear a Kegel weight all day?
faqs.answer: Do not assume that longer use is better. Follow the specific product instructions and a clinician-approved programme; a training tool is not intended to replace normal relaxation throughout the day.
